question: A particular \(12\)-hour digital clock displays the hour and minute of a day. Unfortunately, whenever it is supposed to display a \(1,\) it mistakenly displays a \(9.\) For example, when it is \(1{:}16\) PM the clock incorrectly shows \(9{:}96\) PM. What fraction of the day will the clock show the correct time?
solution:
The clock shows the correct time exactly when the intended display contains no digit \(1\). We can count one \(12\)-hour cycle, since the same pattern repeats in the other half of the day.

Among the hour labels \(1\) through \(12\), the allowable ones are \(2,3,\ldots,9\), giving \(8\) choices. For the minutes, the tens digit can be \(0,2,3,4,5\), giving \(5\) choices, and the units digit can be any digit except \(1\), giving \(9\) choices.

Every combination of these choices is a valid time with no \(1\), and each such time has exactly one hour label and one pair of minute digits. Thus there are
\[
8\cdot5\cdot9=360
\]
correct minute displays out of \(12\cdot60=720\). Each display lasts one minute, so the fraction of the day is
\[
\frac{360}{720}=\boxed{\frac12},
\]
choice \(\boxed{\text{A}}\).
